endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Sponsors should consider transparency throughout the full continuum of 1584 implementation through use, maintenance, and decommission of the AI-enabled device, and 1585 should design the device with transparency in mind from the beginning.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether a documented transparency plan begun at device design improves transparency across implementation, use, maintenance, and decommissioning, and no study documents how often transparency is added late. The recommendation rests on a single FDA draft guidance that uses "should" language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is expert guidance, which may reflect reasoned judgment but does not provide an estimate of effect on transparency, safety, or patient outcomes.

The endorsing source is an FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions. It asks sponsors to consider transparency from design through decommissioning. Draft guidance is nonbinding and may change before it is finalized. Developers who follow it may be better placed for marketing submissions, although no supplied study measures that effect.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-enabled devices developed with and without a documented design-stage transparency plan. Such studies should measure whether users receive accurate information at implementation, whether performance changes are disclosed during maintenance, and whether decommissioning is communicated to clinicians and patients. Descriptive studies of how often transparency documentation is missing at each lifecycle stage would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether transparency materials produced under such a plan would be understandable or usable by their patients and staff.
